candidates.text: Your internet depends on hidden seabed cables.
A break shifts traffic onto other cables.
Deep-sea sections are only about 25 millimetres across.
They weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre on the seabed.
When one breaks, a cable ship must find the fault and splice it at sea.
Submarine fiber-optic cable failed because light pulses travel through fibre pairs inside armoured deep-sea cable about 25 mm across.
What stops if submarine fiber-optic cable stops?

selected.text: Your internet depends on hidden seabed cables.

paragraphs.text: Your internet depends on hidden seabed cables.

Most people never see it. Modern submarine cables are typically about 25 mm in diameter and weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre in deep-sea sections. By 1872 all continents except Antarctica had been linked by submarine telecommunications cables. In 1873 a whale damaged the Persian Gulf Cable between Karachi and Gwadar. Cable ships are limited to about eight knots while laying cable so it settles properly on the sea floor. Eleven breaks occurred on early cables by 1860 because of storms, tides, sand movement and wear on rocks. The Great Eastern laid the first cable to reach India from Aden in 1870. Intercontinental internet and voice traffic runs mostly through fibre cables on the seabed.
Here is how it works. Light pulses travel through fibre pairs inside armoured deep-sea cable about 25 mm across, with repeaters boosting the signal along the route.
That is the bottleneck. A cut cable must be located at sea, lifted and spliced by a specialised cable ship before its capacity returns.
The failure would not stay contained. A break shifts traffic onto other cables; where spare capacity is thin, latency rises and some links slow until the repair ship arrives.
So what protects the system? Route diversity, spare capacity on parallel cables, protection zones near shore and standing repair-ship agreements limit the damage.

miniNarrative: Individual optical fibers are typically coated with various polymer layers and ultimately enclosed by an outer jacket.
The jacketed cable can be routed with no protection or contained in an electrical conduit suitable for the environment where the cable is used.
Different fiber-optic cable types: SMF or MMF, are used for fiber-optic communication in diverse applications: long-distances, connecting parts of a building, or transmitting data across continents.

miniNarrative: A break shifts traffic onto other cables; where spare capacity is thin, latency rises and some links slow until the repair ship arrives.

A fiber-optic cable, also known as an optical-fiber cable, is an assembly that contains one or more optical fibers, glass or polymer, that carry light, with construction similar to an electrical cable.
The infrared light used in telecommunications cannot be seen, so there is a potential laser safety hazard to technicians.
The eye's natural defense against sudden exposure to bright light is the blink reflex, which is not triggered by infrared sources.
shorts.payoff: Small glass fragments can also be a problem if they get under someone's skin, so care is needed to ensure that fragments produced when cleaving fiber are properly collected and disposed of appropriately.
